titulo: Gender and plural: No articles, but with gender

aula.objetivo: Understand that Russian has no articles, find the gender of a noun from its ending and form the regular plural.

blocos.texto: (or: how to tell in three seconds whether a Russian word is masculine, feminine or neuter)

blocos.titulo: The noun: no articles, and gender from the last letter
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: First of all: what is a noun? You have heard the word «noun» a thousand times at school. But let me refresh your memory, because it matters for what comes next. A noun is a word that names. It names things, people, places, ideas, feelings. House. Map. Dog. Friendship. Coffee. Brazil. It is the «who» or the «what» of any sentence. If you can point at something and give it a name, that name is a noun. In English you hardly think about it. You learned the language so naturally that a noun is just one word among others. But when you learn a new language, you need to understand what a noun is, because it is the basis of everything. And in Russian the noun has one property that will determine everything that comes after: gender. STEP 2: The first piece of good news: Russian has no articles. Here you can breathe a sigh of relief. Russian has no articles. Neither definite («the») nor indefinite («a», «an»). Nothing. In English we say «the map» or «a house». The article is a separate little word. In Russian there is none. Дом can mean «house», «the house» or «a house». Context decides. You do not have to worry about any article. Zero. But this raises a question. In English, nouns have no grammatical gender, so you never had to ask who decides it. In Russian every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the adjectives and verbs agree with it. So the inevitable question: who decides the gender? STEP 3: Who decides the Russian gender: the last letter. The direct answer: the last letter of the word. It determines the gender. No article, no exception, no discussion. And here is the second novelty: Russian has three genders, not two. • 1. Masculine — he (он) • 2. Feminine — she (она) • 3. Neuter — it (оно) — the English «it», where things, objects and concepts live. You may have heard that Russian has a «neuter gender». This is it: a third box for the words that are neither masculine nor feminine. Notice that in Russian a table can be «he» and a book can be «she»: gender is a property of the word, not of the thing.

blocos.titulo: Gender from the ending: the table and the three-second rule
blocos.explicacao: The master table: gender from the ending. Here is the rule that solves 95% of cases. Look at the last letter. Apply the table. Done. That is all. Ends in a consonant? Masculine. Ends in -а or -я? Feminine. Ends in -о, -е or -мя? Neuter. Ends in -ь? You need to check the dictionary, and I will explain why in a moment. The three-second protocol. For any new word you meet, do this: • 1. Look at the last letter. • 2. Apply the rule: consonant or -й → masculine -а or -я → feminine -о, -е or -мя → neuter -ь → dictionary • 3. Write the word down together with its gender. Always. Never memorise a Russian word without the gender. The right flashcard is not «дом = house». It is «дом = house (masculine)». The gender always comes with the word, because, as you will see in the next lesson, the adjective depends on it. Does it look simple? It is simple. But there are some traps. And that is what we will talk about now.

blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: TRAP No. 1 — The soft sign (-ь). The -ь (called the «soft sign» or «мягкий знак») is the stone in the Russian learner's shoe. It has no sound of its own. It is not a vowel and not a consonant. It is a sign that softens the consonant before it. Think of it as a «seasoning» that changes the texture of the sound but adds nothing. The problem is that, for gender, it is ambiguous. Some nouns ending in -ь are masculine. Others are feminine. There is no rule and no logic. You have to check the dictionary. See: How do you know? Only by looking in the dictionary. But do not despair. With time you will hear the gender, because the adjectives that go with the word give the game away. A Russian says большо́й день («a big day») and больша́я ночь («a big night»). The ending of the adjective tells you whether it is masculine or feminine. But that is a topic for the next lesson. For now, remember this: -ь means dictionary. Do not try to guess. Check. And write the gender down with the word. STEP 2: TRAP No. 2 — The -мя. Words ending in -мя are neuter. Always. And there are few of them: about ten in the whole Russian language. You do not need to memorise them all at once. The two most used are: имя (EE-mya) — name время (VRYEH-mya) — time, hour The others (знамя, семя, пламя, стремя, племя, темя, бремя, вымя, полымя) are less frequent. But the rule is the same: -мя = neuter. You have just learned the rule for all of them at once. That is what a rule is for: it works even with words you have never seen. STEP 3: TRAP No. 3 — The celebrity кофе. Here is the most famous exception in the Russian language. Ко́фе (KOH-fyeh) — coffee. It ends in -е. By the rule it should be neuter. But it is masculine. Why? History. The word entered Russian as кофий (KOH-fee), which was masculine. Over time the word shrank to кофе, but the gender stayed. It is a linguistic fossil. Remember: вку́сный ко́фе (tasty coffee). Not «вкусное кофе». It is masculine. (Modern grammars tolerate the neuter in informal contexts, but the masculine is the classic, recommended form. Use the masculine.)

In English we say «the book» and «a book». In Russian there is no «the», «a» or «an»: the word «книга» can mean «the book» or «a book», and the context decides. That is why, for every noun, you need to remember the gender (masculine, feminine or neuter). It is the gender that controls the adjective, the possessive and the verb in the past.
blocos.comparacao: the/a/an + noun. In Russian only the noun appears.

exemplos.pt: This is a book / the book.
This is a house / the house.
This is a window / the window.
